switch_statement.quote: It prints only Tue; so the switch jumps to case 2, prints Tue, and then the switch is finished; The other cases are skipped; because they do not match
switch_statement.rule: wrong rule: After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break. Right rule: Without break, all the statements after the matching label run, including those under later case labels, until a break or the end of the switch.

paths.label: shown
paths.quote: It prints only Tue; so the switch jumps to case 2, prints Tue, and then the switch is finished; The other cases are skipped; because they do not match
paths.logic: Folk meaning: everyday 'switch' means flip to one setting, and 'case' reads like 'in case of X do Y', a self-contained rule. Novices therefore expect only the matching case to run. In a Java switch statement, the case labels are only entry points: execution starts at the matching label and falls through the following cases until a break.

paths.label: shown
paths.quote: It prints only Tue; so the switch jumps to case 2, prints Tue, and then the switch is finished; The other cases are skipped; because they do not match
paths.logic: Folk meaning: in everyday instructions a listener reads the whole list at once, does steps in a sensible order and infers what the writer wants. Java instead executes statements one at a time, top to bottom, each only when control reaches it, and nothing later in the program has any effect earlier.
